passage:
Monday, assembly line.
"Straight, Mridul. Sir is looking." Sumit nudged him.
"I am straight. Why do we even stand?"
"Because Sir says."
Mridul stood, mostly thinking about the ruler.
Saturday, at his grandfather's house, the radio began the anthem. Mridul jumped up.
"Nobody's checking, you know," Dada laughed.
"I know," Mridul said, hand at his side. "It feels like saying thank you. Not just a rule."
Dada turned the radio up a little.

qa.q: Who nudged Mridul in the assembly line?
qa.a: Sumit nudged him.

qa.q: What was Mridul mostly thinking about as he stood on Monday?
qa.a: Avoiding trouble: he stood because Sir said so, and he was mostly thinking about the ruler.

qa.q: How can a child move from standing for a rule to standing for a reason?
qa.a: Ask why, and notice what the gesture means to people, as Mridul did when he felt it was a way of saying thank you.

qa.q: How does Dada see Mridul jumping up for the anthem at home?
qa.a: He is amused and probably a little touched, since nobody was checking and Mridul stood by his own choice.

grounding: Illustrates a child standing for the anthem out of school obedience who later feels it as respect.

passage: As the anthem began at the Toronto school assembly, Oskar whispered a silly rhyme about its words. Chen snorted, then held his breath, shoulders shaking. Everyone else in the row stood still. Chen glanced sideways at a girl in the next row, one hand flat on her chest, her eyes shiny. His giggle died. He stared at his shoes until the last note. At recess Oskar started the rhyme again. "Tell me later," Chen said. "Not during the song." Oskar shrugged. "It's just funny." "I know it is," Chen said. "Later."

qa.q: What did Oskar whisper during the anthem?
qa.a: Oskar whispered a silly rhyme about its words.

qa.q: What made Chen stop giggling, and how might he have felt afterwards?
qa.a: He saw a girl with a hand on her chest and shiny eyes, so he realised the anthem mattered a lot to some people; he probably felt a bit sheepish.

qa.q: What could Chen do next time a friend jokes during the anthem?
qa.a: Ask the friend to save the joke for later, as he did, and stay quiet and still himself.

qa.q: How might Oskar see Chen's request?
qa.a: As harmless fun being turned down; Oskar shrugged and said it was just funny, so Oskar may have been a little surprised or put out.

grounding: Illustrates a child giggling at the anthem because friends do, then noticing others' feelings and saving jokes for later.

passage: Sunday. Pradeep Dada told Siddharth about his own elder brother, a soldier who held a mountain post through a snowstorm. Siddharth forgot to blink. "Weren't you scared for him?" "Every day." Wednesday. Siddharth had broken the classroom window with a ball, and the others had run off. His stomach knotted, but he thought of the soldier and walked to the teacher's table to say it was him. Saturday. He joined Dada at the colony clean-up, dragging a sack of leaves. "Soldiers keep the border," he said. "Somebody has to keep the colony."

qa.q: What did Siddharth break?
qa.a: He broke the classroom window with a ball.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling while Dada told the soldier's story?
qa.a: Awe: he forgot to blink and asked whether Dada was scared for his brother.

qa.q: How did Siddharth turn his admiration into action?
qa.a: He told the teacher the truth about the window and joined the colony clean-up.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Dada feel seeing Siddharth at the clean-up?
qa.a: Probably proud and moved, since the story about his brother seems to have reached his grandson.

grounding: Illustrates a child awed by a soldier's story who expresses admiration through honesty and helping the community.

passage:
"You hum the anthem so loudly!" Sarika laughed.
Bhaskar went a bit pink. "I'm new here. In Assam we practised for Republic Day for weeks. I miss it."
"You love it that much?"
"Same as anyone." Bhaskar looked at her. "I just wanted somebody to know."
"Well, I know now." Sarika hooked an arm through his. "We need one more for the flag group. Want to be in?"
"Really?"
"Yes! And you can teach us that song you keep humming."

qa.q: Where is Bhaskar from?
qa.a: He is from Assam.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as the talk went on, and how can you tell?
qa.a: At first she was amused and a little surprised; her warm answers and inviting Bhaskar into the flag group show she welcomed Bhaskar.

qa.q: How can a class welcome a new classmate from another region?
qa.a: Include them in group jobs, ask about their home and listen, as Sarika did with the flag group 🙂.

qa.q: How might Bhaskar feel when Sarika answers?
qa.a: Relieved and included: after saying he wanted somebody to know, he was invited into the flag group.

grounding: Illustrates a classmate from another region saying he loves the country too and being welcomed as a fellow citizen.

passage: Divyansh, you look worried about the loud news at dinner. Sit. I'm your Mama Mohit, and I'll tell you what happened to me at your age. It was election time. My father and my uncle shouted across the table about leaders, so angrily that I stopped eating. I thought, they both say they love this country, so why are they shouting? I went red and kept quiet. The next day I asked my father, softly, what he was most worried about. He told me. Then I asked my uncle the same. They had different answers, and both were really thinking about the country.

qa.q: What season was it when Mohit's father and uncle shouted about leaders?
qa.a: It was election time.

qa.q: What was young Mohit feeling when the elders shouted at the table?
qa.a: He was confused: both men said they loved the country, yet they shouted, and he went red and stopped eating.

qa.q: How could a child respond when elders argue about leaders?
qa.a: Listen, and ask calm questions later, as Mohit did by asking each of them what they were most worried about.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel hearing this story from Mama Mohit?
qa.a: Probably reassured, since even Mama was confused as a child, and Divyansh learns that people can disagree and both still care about the country.

grounding: Illustrates a child confused by elders' angry arguments who asks calm questions and learns disagreement can coexist with love for the country.

passage: My name is Aditi, and this happened in the town park last Independence Day. Ishita and I were standing near the flagpole by the freedom memorial when a man finished his chips and dropped the packet by the base of the pole. My chest went tight. Somebody had just dirtied the place where everyone came to be proud. Ishita whispered, "Leave it, it's not our problem." I waited a second. Then I walked over, picked it up and put it in the dustbin. Ishita said nothing, but at the gate I saw her carrying her own wrapper to the bin.

qa.q: What did the man drop near the flagpole?
qa.a: He dropped a chips packet by the base of the pole.

qa.q: Why did Aditi feel uneasy when the man dropped the packet?
qa.a: Aditi felt the place where everyone came to be proud had just been dirtied, and that made Aditi's chest go tight.

qa.q: What small step could Aditi take if the man were still standing nearby?
qa.a: Aditi could gently remind him, or simply pick up the packet, as Aditi did that day.

qa.q: How might Ishita have seen Aditi's choice?
qa.a: At first Ishita thought it was not their problem, but carrying her own wrapper to the bin later suggests Aditi's action changed her mind 😊.

grounding: Illustrates a child uneasy at litter near a flag who picks it up out of civic respect.

passage: Sunday night. Papa gave me my first weekly pocket money today, fifty rupees, right in my hand like a grown-up. I felt about three metres tall 😊. I nearly ran to buy stickers with all of it. Then I thought about Papa leaving the shop late every evening and Mummy checking bills at the kitchen table. This money is their tired days. So I put twenty in my savings box. I'll spend ten on a pencil for Raghav's birthday and keep the rest for a notebook I actually need. Tomorrow I'll say thank you properly. - Vidya

qa.q: How much pocket money did Vidya receive?
qa.a: Vidya received fifty rupees.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when Papa put the money in Vidya's hand, and what made Vidya think again?
qa.a: Vidya felt grown-up, then thoughtful: Vidya remembered Papa leaving the shop late and Mummy checking bills, so the money felt like their tired days.

qa.q: How could Vidya show that the pocket money is valued?
qa.a: Plan the spending, save some and buy things Vidya really needs, as Vidya's plan already does.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Vidya thanks him properly?
qa.a: Probably proud and touched, because it shows Vidya understands the work behind the money.

grounding: Illustrates a child receiving pocket money who feels grown-up and grateful for the parents' hard work.

passage: Omkar spent his whole week's pocket money on a light-up spinning top in under a minute. Ten minutes later, walking home with Tushar, the top wobbled and its light went dead. Tushar poked it. "You could have got a football pump for that." Omkar's stomach sank. He had wanted a football pump too. The next Saturday a sticker book caught his eye at the same stall. His hand went to his pocket and stopped. "Tomorrow," he told himself. By Sunday he had forgotten the sticker book and dropped the coins into his box instead.

qa.q: What did Omkar buy with his week's pocket money?
qa.a: He bought a light-up spinning top.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when the top's light went dead?
qa.a: Regret: his stomach sank, because he had also wanted a football pump.

qa.q: What small step helped Omkar the next Saturday?
qa.a: He told himself "tomorrow" and waited a day before buying, and by then he no longer wanted the sticker book.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the moment with the dead top?
qa.a: As a friend pointing out what else the money could have bought, probably without meaning to hurt, since Tushar just poked the top.

grounding: Illustrates a child spending all his allowance on impulse, feeling regret, and learning to wait a day.

passage:
"Count it again," Ganga said.
"It's all there." Tushar tipped the coin box onto the shop counter. "Eight months of Sundays."
"You never spent it?"
"I almost bought a kite in June."
The shopkeeper set the cricket bat down. "Hold it."
Tushar's hands were shaking a little. "Mine. I paid for it myself."
Ganga grinned. "You'll sleep with it tonight."
"Maybe." He gripped the handle. "It feels heavier than it looked."
"That's the eight months," said Ganga.

qa.q: What did Tushar almost buy in June?
qa.a: He almost bought a kite in June.

qa.q: What does the shaking of Tushar's hands suggest he feels?
qa.a: Deep pride and excitement about holding a bat he paid for with his own saved money.

qa.q: What does Tushar's eight months of saving show about effort?
qa.a: That patience and steady effort can build something he wants, even when spending sooner is tempting 🙂.

qa.q: How might Ganga see the moment at the counter?
qa.a: With warm amusement and pride in Tushar, as Ganga teases him about sleeping with the bat and says the bat feels heavier because of the eight months.

grounding: Illustrates a child proud after saving for months to buy a cricket bat with his own money.

passage: At the tea stall outside the kasba school, Devika bought a jalebi, a balloon, a packet of peanuts and a ribbon, all at once. Wasim watched, two rupees warm in his fist. Something pinched in his chest. He looked at Devika's shiny new pencil case and then at the corner of his own, cracked but neat. He remembered Abba's sewing machine humming late, and Ammi tucking a boiled egg into his bag that morning. Devika held out the jalebi. "Half?" Wasim hesitated, then broke off a piece. "Thanks," he said, and this time the pinch in his chest was small.

qa.q: How many rupees did Wasim have in his fist?
qa.a: He had two rupees in his fist.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he watched Devika buy things, and what helped it shrink?
qa.a: He felt a pinch of envy; remembering Abba's sewing machine and Ammi's boiled egg reminded him of what his own family gives, and the pinch grew small.

qa.q: How can Wasim cope when a friend has more pocket money?
qa.a: Remember that families differ and value what he has, instead of comparing, as he did.

qa.q: How might Devika see the moment at the stall?
qa.a: Devika probably had no idea Wasim felt a pinch; Devika was enjoying the treats and offered to share half of the jalebi.

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling envy at a friend's larger pocket money and settling it by remembering his own family's gifts.
